voice_event.speaker: desert
voice_event.text: Three things. The first reordered our lives. One command, heard as though it were spoken straight to you: sell what you have, give it to the poor, and follow me. Not a saying to be studied - an order to be obeyed. The second we argued for, when we were pressed to. The Word of God was not changed, but took a human body for our salvation, so that by sharing human birth he might make us share the divine nature. That is the reason we gave for why he came at all. And we did not think this rested on our say-so. Read the accounts, we told those who came to test us, and see that the deeds of Christ prove him to be God come to earth for our salvation. The third is what we thought his cross had already done. The old oracles fell silent when it rose. The knowledge of God spread. And death stopped being the thing that could make a person do anything. That is why, when persecution ended and dying for the faith was no longer asked of us, we did not think we had been let off. The same fight had moved inward, against our own thoughts rather than against the sword.

voice_event.text: He took a human body for our salvation, so that by sharing our birth he might make us share what is his. That is the reason we gave for why he came at all. His cross made the old oracles fall silent, spread the knowledge of God, and broke death's power to make a person do anything. We said this to the devil's own face: your coming, Christ, has made you weak, cast you down, and stripped you. The healings that happened among us were not ours - we are not the doers of these things, one of us told the philosophers who had just watched him sign the cross over a man; it is Christ who works them, by means of those who believe in him. His deeds prove him to be God come to earth for our salvation, we told anyone who tested us. Read the accounts and see. Beyond that accounting - how his death reaches you in particular, a worked-out system of penalty and substitution - we did not write that down. What we have is what he did, not a theory of how it operates.

voice_event.text: Stillness: quiet of body and mind, sought as both the condition and the fruit of the ascetic life. It was not a technique we systematized, the way some later traditions did. What we can tell you is that one current among us spoke of it as something actually reached - a soul filled with light, made the Spirit's own seat, known in real experience and feeling, not only believed. The soul in communion with the Spirit of his light becomes all light, all face, all eye, with no part of her not full of the spiritual eyes of light. The Spirit of the Lord himself becomes, for souls that are worthy, their rest, their joy, their delight. Another of our teachers defined the kingdom itself as apatheia - freedom from the passions - together with true knowledge of beings. Both spoke of stillness as something that could be reached, not merely aimed at. We will not promise you that most of us reached it. What we can say is that it was named, taught, and held as real.

sources.author: Pseudo-Macarius - the attribution the Internet Archive itself uses for this very item ('by Pseudo-Macarius; Macarius, the Egyptian, Saint, 4th cent; Mason, Arthur James, 1851-1928'), leading with the ascription Mason spent his Introduction arguing against. sources.author: Evagrius Ponticus (c. 345-399 CE) - Greek-educated theologian formed under the Cappadocians, at Kellia from c. 385 to his death; this world's most systematic participant-author and its most atypical by education
sources.work: Praktikos; Chapters on Prayer (De oratione); Antirrhetikos - the most systematic surviving interior psychology of the ascetic life produced inside this world (Strand C, Kellia): the eight logismoi, apatheia, the practice of talking back to thoughts with Scripture. Transmission is this world's starkest survival story: after the 553 condemnation (well outside this world's own window), the speculative works survive chiefly in Syriac and Armenian; in Greek, Chapters on Prayer transmits mostly under the name of Nilus of Ancyra, while the Praktikos generally transmits under Evagrius's own name
sources.locus: Praktikos chs. 2-3, in Luke Dysinger's English (cic/texts/evagrius_praktikos_dysinger.txt)
sources.rights_status: MIXED, and this source is the first in the fleet where that matters. The ancient works are public-domain in their surviving versions. The vendored Praktikos is NOT: Dysinger's English is a modern translation, a derivative work in which he holds copyright, carried here under the Guide to Evagrius Ponticus's own CC BY 4.0 licence and its editor's statement that the Guide includes 'only those versions without license restrictions'. CC BY is a grant with a condition: attribution must travel with anything quoted. The Guide's own Bridgeman/Droz reasoning covers the ANCIENT-LANGUAGE main texts of critical editions and does NOT reach an English translation - no record here may call this text public domain. Chapters on Prayer and the Antirrhetikos remain unvendored, their modern English copyrighted and consult-only.

results.message: Why did your people believe this?

voice_event.speaker: desert
voice_event.text: We believed it because we held it as the reason he came at all - the Word took a human body for our salvation, so that by sharing our birth he might make us share what is his. That was not a teaching we invented. We took it from the accounts themselves: read them, we told those who tested us, and see that the deeds of Christ prove him to be God come to earth for our salvation. The cross made the old oracles fall silent, spread the knowledge of God, and broke death's power. We saw that in our own time - people no longer feared death the way they had. When persecution ended and dying for the faith was no longer asked of anyone, we understood the same total struggle to have moved inward, against our own thoughts rather than against the sword. The enemy we fought there was one Christ had already beaten. That is why we said to the devil's own face: your coming, Christ, has made you weak, cast you down, and stripped you. We believed it because we had seen its effects, not only because we had been told it.

confidence.divergence_note: Widely Accepted for the narrated material (Antony's call, his own reported teaching) and its place in this world's own tradition. Contested for the SS72-80 disputation specifically: the Vita's own editor flags at that point how startling it is to find Antony 'reasoning with philosophers upon the doctrines of Neoplatonism', and the argument's vocabulary tracks Athanasius's own de Incarnatione - what is certain is that the tradition put these words in Antony's mouth, not that he spoke them. Each quote record carries that bound in its own divergence_note. This witness still does not claim a systematic Christology worked out as argument for its own sake; see desert.limit.doubt-and-doctrine for the narrowed bound.
